doc.title: Jane Jarvis interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995

title: Duke Ellington's keyboard harmony
summary: Her Bush Conservatory teacher said Ellington knew more keyboard harmony than anyone; she explains his orchestral piano approach.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: than any living person. Now of course this was many years ago. I wasn’t too sure of what she meant until I began to study what he did. Because so many people think a pianist is a person that plays, you know lots of little frills or lots and lots of heavy rhythm, or a combination. I’m talking about early concepts now of jazz. Whereas Duke looked upon the piano as an orchestral instrument. And you know once in a while he’d play an arpeggio. But he wasn’t known for whooping around all over the notes. He made every note important. My piano teacher said, “He knows how to get from here to there with the least commotion.”

He had such a solid knowledge of what chords constitute, uh, what constitutes chords, and their different positions, that he could play what it would take anybody else twenty minutes to do, to get from here to there you know. And at that point, when she said that, it didn’t really, it was too big to grasp. Because piano just wasn’t played that way. So at any rate, what was I talking about?
We were talking about people that you were listening to and maybe absorbing.
Unfortunately, well there weren’t too many women pianists that came to the fore, because it just was unthinkable. Women were supposed to be in the more sedate careers.
